description: Hi, I'm Priya, an AI engineer in Bengaluru with 7+ yrs in GenAI, multi-agent systems (LangGraph), RAG, Python/FastAPI/React & data pipelines. 4 research papers, SIH finalist. Building an AI "Earth Trend Detective" that analyzes NASA data & explains environmental change. I'll handle AI/backend, with a clear plan from hour one. Looking for: Earth science/remote sensing, frontend/UI & maps, data viz, demo video/storytelling. All levels welcome. Let's build a winner! 🚀
summary: Climate headlines talk about global averages, but people care about their own place. Is my city getting hotter at night? Are the rains coming back to the Sahel? Trend Detective is a free web app that lets anyone, students included, click a point on Earth and put it “on trial” using 45 years of NASA data. A two-question wizard suggests variables in plain language. The app then pulls MERRA-2 and CERES data live from NASA POWER and runs two independent tests: a straight-line test corrected for autocorrelation, and the Mann-Kendall rank test with Sen’s slope. The result is a clear verdict: Case Closed, Open Case or Inconclusive. When a trend isn’t clear yet, the app estimates how many more years of data would be needed to detect it. A regional grid shows the same variable rising in one place and falling in another. Guided case files teach the method, and a personal casebook lets users save their investigations, return to any earlier step and sync across devices. Every result can be checked against an independent Python and SciPy engine. Trend Detective makes climate statistics something anyone can explore, while staying scientifically honest.
details:
Climate news usually reports global averages, but people want to know about their own place. Is my city getting hotter at night? Is the rain coming back to the Sahel? Is the snow in the Arctic disappearing? Trend Detective is a free web app that lets anyone, from a school student to a researcher, put any point on Earth “on trial” and ask NASA’s data whether it is really changing or just wiggling.

  1. Pick a place. Click anywhere on a NASA GIBS Blue Marble / Black Marble map.
    • an OLS linear trend with a 95% confidence interval, corrected for autocorrelation (Santer et al. 2000);
    • a Mann-Kendall rank test with Sen’s slope, also corrected for autocorrelation (Yue & Wang 2004).
    • A Pettitt change-point test tells a steady ramp apart from a sudden jump.
  2. The verdict. You get a plain-language result: “Case closed”, “Open case” or “Inconclusive”.
  3. Years-until-significant meter. When a trend isn’t significant yet, the app doesn’t just say “no”. Using Weatherhead et al. (1998), it estimates how many more years of data would be needed to detect the trend reliably, with an uncertainty range.
  4. Regional trend map. A grid of up to 7×7 points, each tested separately. It shows that the same variable can rise in one place and fall a few hundred kilometres away.

Other features:

  • Analysis options: yearly averages, all months with the seasonal cycle removed, single seasons (DJF/MAM/JJA/SON) or single months.
  • Three views: trend chart, climate stripes, and a month × year anomaly heat map.
  • Guided case files: five auto-playing investigations (The Melting North, Sahel: Return of the Rains?, Rising Here Falling There, The Patient Detective, Hot Nights in the City).
  • My Cases casebook: save investigations with notes and checkpoints, and sync them across devices with a casebook code. No login is needed.
  • Verify with Python: sends the exact series to an independent FastAPI + SciPy engine and shows both results side by side. They agree to about 10⁻¹⁵.
  • CSV download and shareable links.

Benefits

  • Accessible: no login, no install and no coding. Two clicks take you from curiosity to a scientifically tested answer.
  • Honest statistics: autocorrelation is corrected, two independent methods must agree, and “we can’t tell yet” is a valid, quantified answer instead of a false yes or no.
  • Local relevance: any coordinate on Earth, not just a global average.
  • Transparent and checkable: every method is cited, and results can be verified against SciPy with one click.

Intended impact
We want to build climate and data literacy, especially among students and teachers. Users learn that a trend is a statistical claim that needs evidence, that natural variability can hide real change, and that climate change looks different from place to place. By making “Is this real?” a question anyone can answer with NASA data, Trend Detective helps fight both alarmism and denial with evidence. It also introduces a wider audience to NASA’s open Earth science datasets.

Tools, languages and software

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet / React-Leaflet and Recharts, hosted on Netlify. All statistics run in the browser, so the app works with no server at all.
  • Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, NumPy and SciPy, deployed with Docker on Render. It is an independent reference engine with /api/analyze, /api/trend and /api/region endpoints.
  • Data and storage: NASA POWER monthly point API (GMAO MERRA-2 meteorology, CERES radiation and clouds) and NASA GIBS imagery. Netlify Functions and Netlify Blobs handle casebook sync, with localStorage for offline use.
  • Testing: Vitest and pytest. One shared test fixture keeps the TypeScript and Python engines in agreement, and the Python engine is unit-tested against scipy.stats.linregress and theilslopes.
  • AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped with code and text. All statistical methods are cited and verified by tests.
  • Hardware: standard laptops only, since the whole system runs on public cloud and open NASA APIs.

How the project is creative

  • Detective metaphor: a statistics workflow becomes a story, with cases, clues, two detectives, verdict stamps and a casebook. This makes hypothesis testing intuitive and fun.
  • “Not yet” is an answer: the Years-until-significant meter turns a non-significant result into a forward-looking finding. It teaches that detecting a trend depends on noise and record length, an idea rarely shown to the public.
  • Rising Here, Falling There: the regional grid shows spatial differences directly, instead of hiding them in a single number.
  • Two engines, one answer: a browser engine and a Python engine check each other, so trust is earned openly rather than assumed.

Factors our team considered

  • Statistical rigor: monthly climate data is autocorrelated, so a plain t-test would overstate significance. We corrected for this and required two independent tests to agree.
  • Audience: plain language, kid-friendly variable definitions and guided case files for beginners, plus the full numbers (slopes, confidence intervals, p-values, effective sample size) for experts.
  • Seasonality: the seasonal cycle can be removed, or a single season or month analysed, so that summer and winter trends aren’t mixed together.
  • Data limits: CERES data starts in 1984, incomplete years are dropped, and missing values (−999) are handled.
  • Reliability and cost: no paid database and no required backend. Results are cached, NASA POWER requests have a proxy plus a direct fallback, and the regional grid limits how many requests run at once to be polite to NASA’s shared public service.
  • Accessibility and colour: each variable gets a matching diverging palette (brown↔teal for water, blue↔red for heat). Faded cells mean “not significant yet”, so meaning doesn’t depend on colour alone.
  • Privacy: no accounts and no personal data collected.

What’s next: comparing trends between two places, more datasets (GPM IMERG, MODIS NDVI, GRACE groundwater), a teacher mode with worksheets, and offline case files.
